how does your tool set compare to claude code?

Good question! My tool set is very similar to Claude Code's, with strong overlap in the core capabilities. Here's a comparison:

I'm constrained to a sandbox VM — no git push, no GitHub CLI writes

Overall, the day-to-day workflow is nearly identical: read, edit, search, run commands, track tasks, and delegate. The main gaps are web search and notebook editing.

What does a jupyter notebook do? 

Pondered · 15s

A Jupyter Notebook is an interactive, web-based document that combines:

Live code execution — You write code in cells and run them one at a time, seeing output immediately
Narrative text — Markdown cells for explanations, documentation, and commentary
Rich output — Tables, charts, plots, images, and even interactive widgets inline alongside the code
Key Characteristics
Cell-based — Content is organized into cells (code cells or markdown cells) that can be run independently or all together
Kernel-backed — A language "kernel" (commonly Python, but also R, Julia, etc.) runs the code behind the scenes and maintains state between cell executions
Stateful — Variables and data persist across cells — you can define a variable in one cell and use it in the next
.ipynb format — Notebooks are stored as JSON files with the .ipynb extension, embedding code, output, and metadata together
Common Use Cases
Data science & analysis — Exploring datasets, cleaning data, building models
Education — Teaching programming with a mix of explanation and runnable examples
Prototyping — Quick experimentation with ideas before turning them into scripts
Reports — Sharing reproducible analyses with narrative, code, and results in one document

The name "Jupyter" comes from Julia, Python, and R — the three languages it originally supported, though it now works with many more.

what do you do with it? 

Marinated · 12s

With a Jupyter notebook, here's what I can and can't do:

What I Can Do
Read .ipynb files — They're just JSON, so my read tool shows the full contents
Edit them — I can use write or edit to modify the JSON structure directly (add/remove cells, change code or markdown)
Run them — If the environment has Jupyter installed, I can execute notebooks via bash (e.g., jupyter nbconvert --execute notebook.ipynb or jupyter execute)
Search them — grep and glob work on .ipynb files like any other file
What I Can't Do (That Claude Code Can)
NotebookEdit — Claude Code has a dedicated tool that understands notebook cell structure natively, making it easier to insert, replace, or delete specific cells without manually wrangling JSON
In Practice

If you asked me to work on a notebook, I'd:

Read the .ipynb file to understand its structure
Edit the JSON directly to make changes (a bit more manual but works fine)
Run it through Jupyter if execution is needed
Read the output back to verify results

It's slightly less convenient than a native notebook-editing tool, but entirely functional for most tasks. Want me to try working on one?

what does claude use it for? 

Simmered · 11s

Claude Code's NotebookEdit tool is used specifically for working with Jupyter notebooks in a more structured way. Here's what it does:

Core Use Cases

1. Cell-level editing without JSON wrangling Instead of manually parsing and modifying the .ipynb JSON structure, NotebookEdit understands notebooks natively. You can tell it:

"Insert a new cell after cell 3 with this code"
"Replace cell 5's content with this markdown"
"Delete cell 2"

2. Three edit modes

Insert — Add a new cell at a specific position
Replace — Swap out a cell's content
Delete — Remove a cell entirely

3. Cell type awareness You specify whether a cell is a code cell or a markdown cell, and the tool handles the formatting correctly.

Why It Exists

The practical problem it solves: .ipynb files are complex JSON with nested structures (cells, source, metadata, outputs, execution_count, etc.). Editing them with a plain text tool means:

Risk of breaking the JSON structure
Difficulty targeting one cell among many
Managing line-by-line source arrays (Jupyter stores cell content as arrays of strings)

NotebookEdit abstracts all that away, so Claude Code can manipulate notebooks at the cell level cleanly.

Realistic Scenarios
A data scientist asks Claude to "add a cell that loads the CSV and shows the first 5 rows"
"Add a markdown cell explaining what the next code block does"
"Remove the broken cell and replace it with a fixed version"

Without it, you'd do the same work — just with more manual JSON editing, which is what I'd do in this environment.

does claude actually do that often? 

Philosophised · 12s

Honestly, not very often. Here's the reality:

In Practice

Jupyter notebooks are a niche use case for Claude Code. The vast majority of Claude Code sessions involve standard software development — working with .py, .ts, .js, .tsx files, running builds, tests, etc. Notebooks just don't come up frequently in that workflow.

Why It's Rare
Claude Code's audience is mostly software engineers working on codebases — not data scientists in Jupyter
Notebooks are typically interactive — people use them in a live Jupyter/Lab session, not via a CLI coding agent
Data science workflows tend to be exploratory and visual — you want to see plots render, iterate on cells in real time, which a terminal-based agent isn't the best fit for
Most production code lives in .py files, not notebooks
When It Does Come Up
Someone has a notebook in their repo they want to modify
A data scientist specifically wants Claude to help build or fix a notebook
Cleaning up or restructuring an existing notebook

But these are the exception, not the rule. It's one of those tools that exists for completeness — useful when you need it, but most sessions never touch it.

The Bigger Picture

The same is true for me. If you're testing this provider for typical coding tasks — building features, fixing bugs, refactoring, running tests — notebook support won't be the gap you feel. The tools that matter day-to-day (read, edit, bash, grep, search, task delegation) are all here and work the same way.
